blocks.markdown: Today's big question: how does electricity flow?
blocks.say: Today we explore electricity. How does it flow, and how do we use it safely?

blocks.alt: A glowing filament light bulb in the dark
blocks.caption: A bulb turns electrical energy into light and heat.
blocks.credit: Photo by Rodion Kutsaiev on Unsplash
blocks.say: A glowing bulb turns electrical energy into light and some heat.

blocks.markdown:
A **circuit** is a loop that electricity flows around.

It must be **complete**, with no gaps, for the bulb to light.
blocks.say: Electricity is a form of energy that flows around a loop. A loop of wire joined to a power source is called a circuit. The power source can be a cell, which is what we often call a battery. A bulb, a buzzer or a motor in the loop is a component that uses the energy. For the bulb to light, the circuit must be complete, with no gaps. If there is a gap anywhere, the electricity cannot flow and the bulb stays off.

scenes.caption: A complete circuit works.
scenes.say: This circuit has a cell, wires and a bulb joined in a complete loop. The bulb lights up.

scenes.caption: A gap stops the flow.
scenes.say: Here a wire has come loose, so there is a gap. The electricity cannot flow, and the bulb stays off.

question.prompt: A bulb in a circuit will not light. What could be wrong?
question.explanation: Electricity can only flow if the circuit is complete, with no gaps.

options.text: There is a gap in the circuit

blocks.markdown:
A **switch** opens or closes a circuit.

Closed switch: the bulb is on. Open switch: the bulb is off.
blocks.say: A switch is a way to open or close a circuit. When the switch is closed, the gap is joined up, so electricity flows and the bulb lights. When the switch is open, there is a gap, so the bulb goes off. Every light switch at home works this way. It lets us control a circuit without pulling wires apart.

scenes.caption: Closed switch: lamp on.
scenes.say: The switch is closed. The circuit is complete, so the lamp is on.

scenes.caption: Open switch: lamp off.
scenes.say: The switch is open. There is a gap, so the lamp is off.

question.prompt: When a switch is open, the bulb is on.
question.explanation: An open switch makes a gap, so the bulb is off.

blocks.title: Lights on at Fatima's house
blocks.transcript: A cell, wires and a bulb make a circuit. Electricity flows round the loop. A wire comes loose. The loop has a gap and the bulb goes out. A switch opens and closes the circuit. Closed means the bulb is on. A copper wire is a conductor. Electricity flows through metals easily. A wooden spoon is an insulator. The bulb stays off. Two cells give more energy. The bulb shines more brightly. Water conducts electricity. Never touch a plug with wet hands. Fatima switches off the light and fan when she leaves. That saves electricity.

blocks.text: Stop 1: Which materials let electricity through?

blocks.caption: Copper is a metal and a good conductor.
blocks.credit: Photo by Ra Dragon on Unsplash
blocks.say: Metals such as copper are good conductors, so wires have a metal centre.

blocks.markdown:
An electrical **conductor** lets electricity flow through it. Metals are conductors.

An electrical **insulator** does not. Plastic, rubber, wood and glass are insulators.
blocks.say: Some materials let electricity flow through them easily. These are called electrical conductors. Metals such as copper, iron and aluminium are good conductors. That is why wires have a metal centre. Other materials do not let electricity flow. These are called electrical insulators. Plastic, rubber, wood and glass are insulators. That is why wires are covered in plastic, and why a plug has a plastic case. Look at which materials are which.

scenes.caption: Copper conducts.
scenes.say: A copper wire completes the circuit and the bulb lights. Copper is a conductor.

scenes.caption: Wood does not conduct.
scenes.say: A wooden spoon is put in the gap instead. The bulb stays off, because wood is an insulator.

blocks.title: Conductor or insulator?
blocks.goal: Put conductors in one group and insulators in the other.
blocks.say: Now you can test materials yourself. This is a comparative test, which means we compare different things. To make the test fair, we change only the material. Everything else stays the same: the same cell, the same bulb and the same wires. If the bulb lights, the material in the gap is a conductor. Use a battery-powered kit, never the mains.

blocks.text: Stop 1: Add more to the circuit

blocks.markdown:
More cells make a bulb **brighter**.

More bulbs on one cell make each bulb **dimmer**.
blocks.say: What happens if you add more bulbs or more cells? More bulbs sharing one cell each shine more dimly. More cells make the bulb shine more brightly, because there is more energy. A buzzer in the loop makes a sound instead of light, and a motor makes something spin. Different components turn electrical energy into different things.

scenes.say: Two cells and one bulb. The bulb is brighter, because there is more energy.

scenes.say: One cell and two bulbs. Each bulb is dimmer, because they share the energy.

blocks.alt: Power pylons carrying cables across a field at sunset
blocks.caption: Pylons carry mains electricity. Stay far away from them.
blocks.credit: Photo by Matthew Henry on Unsplash
blocks.say: Pylons carry mains electricity across the country. Never go near them.

blocks.markdown:
**Mains** electricity is strong and can be dangerous.

Water conducts electricity, so keep electrical things away from it.
blocks.say: The electricity in our homes comes from the mains. It is much stronger than the electricity in a small cell, and it can hurt or even kill. Never play with plugs, sockets or wires, and never poke anything into a socket. Water is a good conductor, so never touch electrical things with wet hands. Never fly a kite near pylons or overhead power lines. If someone is in danger, do not touch them. Switch off the power if it is safe, or call a grown-up for help.

blocks.alt: Plugs, sockets and wet hands are dangerous together.
blocks.caption: Plugs, sockets and wet hands are dangerous together.
blocks.say: Sockets, plugs and wet hands do not mix with electricity.

blocks.title: My energy saving plan
instructions: Walk around your home. List five things that use electricity.
For each one, write how we could save electricity.
Choose one change to try for a week and tell your family.
blocks.say: Electricity costs money and often comes from burning fuels, which can harm the environment. So we should use it wisely. We should switch off lights and fans when we leave. We should unplug chargers we are not using. We can also use energy saving LED bulbs. In Pakistan, where power cuts can happen, saving electricity helps the whole family. Make a plan for your home.

blocks.say: Switching off lights and fans when no one is using them saves energy.
